newsitem.title: ITALY: INTERVIEW -- Alleanza first 5-mth premiums up 20 pct.
newsitem.headline: INTERVIEW -- Alleanza first 5-mth premiums up 20 pct.

text.p: Italy's largest life insurance group Alleanza Assicurazioni SpA said on Wednesday its premium income for the first five months of 1997 rose around 20 percent and premiums from new policies increased 35 percent.

Alleanza's chairman Alfonso Desiata said in an interview with Reuters that strong growth seen in the current year to end-May had pushed Alleanza's share of the national life insurance market to 12 percent, and ahead of INA.

He said premium growth had been driven by the group's joint venture with Banco Ambrosiano Veneto in which the bank's branches sell Alleanza products, and also better returns from its policies compared to low yields on government bonds.

In mid-May, Alleanza reported that parent company first quarter 1997 premium income rose 21.4 percent and growth from new policies rose 35.3 percent. This followed premium income growth of 11.9 percent for the whole of 1996 compared to 1995.

Alleanza's premium income at the end of 1996 amounted to some 3.129 trillion lire ($1.8 billion), and Desiata says the group aims for five trillion lire by the end of the decade, giving an average annual growth rate of around 12 percent.
"Our objective is to see an average annual 12 percent rise in premium income to the year 2000, while at the same time bringing costs down," said Desiata in the interview.

He added that Alleanza's general expenses for running its headquarters were 2.5 percent in 1996, the lowest in Europe, while commission costs were also very low. Overall group costs were running at around 10 percent of premium income.

Premium business has been driven by Alleanza's Ambroveneto venture which now accounts for five percent of premiums written. With the bank's branches based in the prosperous north-east of Italy, he said this was bringing in "good quality customers".
Desiata said premium income from the joint venture leapt 100 percent in the first quarter of 1997, and expects these premiums to account soon for 6-7 percent of the group's total premiums.

Talks over a merger between Ambroveneto and Italy's largest savings bank Cariplo could only be positive for Alleanza as the combined group would have the largest number of branches in Italy -- some 2,500 -- through which to sell Alleanza products.

Desiata however declined to comment on whether Alleanza, which has a 16 percent stake in Ambroveneto, would subscribe to the planned Ambroveneto rights issue set to finance the Cariplo deal, but he hinted that Alleanza wanted to participate in the business with Cariplo.

He saw great potential from the start-up of individual private pensions in Italy with regulations expected to be approved by the end of 1997. These private schemes are hoped to take pressure off Italy's bloated public pensions system.

Alleanza already has plans underway to launch its own schemes with a target for the year 2000 to include 28,000 policies bringing in around 40-50 billion lire of premiums and be runnng at breakeven by the end of the decade.

Desiata shrugged off the effects of margin pressures on Alleanza's business from Italian interest rates at a 22 year-low, inflation at its lowest level for 28 years and the nation suffering two quarters of negative economic growth.

He pointed out that although in 1996 Alleanza's first year policy lapse rate had risen 1.2 points to 7.52 percent and latter year lapses were up 1.4 points to 7.95 percent, this was lower than the average for Italian insurers at 10-12 percent, although it was worse than Alleanza's 3-4 percent lapse rate in the early 1990's. ($1=1,700 lire)
